Concrete Repair in Celebration, FL

Published 2026-09-11 · By the Kissimmee Concrete team

Celebration · Osceola County

The short version for Celebration

Concrete repair in Celebration is mostly three things: the garage slab edge where the alley apron meets it, sidewalk and walk panels lifted by the street oaks, and cracked lanai slabs being prepared for a paver or travertine overlay. Crack routing and grinding is a minimum-charge visit; a replaced panel runs at new-pour rates ($8.50–$13.50 per sq ft) plus removal. Visible repairs on the street side are noted to the ARC; the county needs no permit for same-footprint repair.

Where Celebration concrete fails

The 1996–2006 homes have concrete garage slabs meeting paver aprons at the alley; the slab edge spalls and the last foot cracks where the apron settled and the expansion joint was never installed. Public sidewalk panels along the tree-lined streets lift 1 to 2 inches at live oaks; those panels are in the community's and county's domain and we repair them under the right approval. Lanai slabs poured with the pool in 2000 have shrinkage cracks that are fine to overlay and, occasionally, a heaved corner at the coping that is not (Resurface vs. Replace). Well-water rust is rare here because Celebration is on utility water; the stains we see are tannin from the oaks, treated differently (Rust Stains From Well-Water Irrigation: Identify, Remove, Prevent).

Approvals

Same-footprint repair needs no county permit. A replaced sidewalk panel in the public strip is county right-of-way and community streetscape, so both the Building Office (407-742-0200) and Town Hall (407-566-1200 ext. 2206) are told; a garage-edge repair behind the house is maintenance. The new concrete will be lighter for a year, which is why we note visible repairs to the ARC. Pages: Celebration (CROA), Unincorporated Osceola County.

Worked example

A garage-edge repair at an alley apron

The last 3 feet of a 20-foot-wide garage slab spalled and cracked where the apron settled; apron relaid on a rebuilt base (see the alley apron example), slab edge saw-cut and removed (60 square feet, $120 to $240), new 4-inch section doweled to the slab and poured at $8.50 to $13.50 ($510 to $810), expansion joint installed at the apron. One day. Ranges from the Q3 2026 index.

Who fixes the lifted public sidewalk in front of my Celebration house?

It is in the county's right-of-way and the community's streetscape, so the answer depends on what lifted it and who is responsible for the tree; Town Hall is the first call. When the owner takes it on, we repair the panel under the county's right-of-way rules and the ARC's streetscape standard, with a root barrier so it does not lift again.

Ageing

A twenty-five-year-old community's concrete is at an age

The first Celebration homes were occupied in 1996 and the build-out ran into the 2010s, so the oldest flatwork in the community is approaching thirty years and the newest is fifteen. Concrete at that age on Osceola's fine sand shows a consistent set of things: joint edges spalled where they were cut shallow, hairline map cracking on south-facing slabs, panel settlement where a downspout or an irrigation line has been running under an edge, and lifted sections where a street tree has matured.

Almost none of that is a failure of the original work. It is what flatwork does here after a quarter century, and the question is which parts are worth replacing now and which will last another decade. We tap-test and string-line each panel and give you the map rather than a single number, because on a Celebration lot the front walk and the driveway apron often need different answers.

Matching, approvals and the alternative to matching

New concrete next to twenty-five-year-old concrete does not match, and on a street with a designed appearance that matters more than usual. There are three honest options. Replace the whole element so it is uniform, which costs more but looks intentional. Replace the failed section and accept a lighter panel for a year or two while it weathers in. Or change the element to pavers, which sidesteps the matching problem and is often already in the approved palette.

The third option is why so many Celebration repair enquiries end as paver jobs. It needs architectural approval, which the second option usually does not, so the timeline changes. We price all three and let the committee calendar inform the choice; the submission contents are on the packet checklist.

On this job

What a tap test on a Celebration lanai finds

The lanai slabs on these homes are typically original and are restrained on at least two sides, by the house and by the screen enclosure footer. That restraint concentrates movement at the joint between them, so the crack we most often find runs along the footer line rather than across the slab. It is usually tight, level and cosmetic, and the right answer is to route and seal it rather than replace anything.

Where the tap test finds a hollow area it is almost always at the outside corner furthest from the house, which is where roof water from the enclosure has been discharging for twenty years. That one is a base problem and the repair starts with the water.

Right-sized fix

Sealing rather than replacing a cosmetic crack

On a restrained lanai slab a tight, level crack along the enclosure footer is doing what the slab is supposed to do, which is relieve stress in one predictable place. Replacing the slab to remove it usually produces another crack in the same location within a few years.

The right treatment is to route it to a clean profile and fill it with a flexible polyurethane sealant that moves with the slab, in a colour matched to the concrete. It is a modest job, it keeps water out of the base, and it looks like a joint rather than like a repair.

Questions we get about this

Do repairs need ARC approval?

Visible ones are noted to the committee because new concrete is lighter for a year; maintenance behind the house is not reviewed.

Can you overlay a cracked lanai slab?

Shrinkage cracks, yes, routed and filled first. A heaved corner at the coping is repaired before any overlay.

What causes the garage-edge cracks?

The alley apron settling with no expansion joint between apron and slab; the fix is both.

Is a permit needed?

Not for same-footprint repair; sidewalk panels in the public strip are confirmed with the county.

Will a replaced concrete panel match the rest?

Not at first. New concrete is lighter for roughly a year and never matches a twenty-five-year-old slab exactly. Replacing the whole element or switching to pavers avoids the problem.

Does a concrete repair need architectural approval?

A like-for-like repair usually does not. Changing the material or the appearance does.
